app-router-model.unlock: You can trace any URL to its page file and name every special file that wraps it, in nesting order.

app-router-model.text: A new hire adds app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx and the page 404s, while a sibling route mysteriously shows the wrong header. Nobody can say which layout is even in play for a given URL. The App Router is a filesystem-to-route compiler with strict conventions, and guessing at it wastes an afternoon per bug. This lesson makes the URL→files mapping something you compute, not divine.

In the Next.js App Router, the app/ directory IS the route table. Each folder is a URL segment; a folder becomes routable only when it contains a page.tsx (or page.js). Special files — layout.tsx, loading.tsx, error.tsx, not-found.tsx, template.tsx — apply to their segment AND every nested segment below. Rendering a URL means finding the deepest folder with a page, then wrapping that page in every layout from the root down. Folders wrapped in parentheses like (marketing) are route groups: organizational, not part of the URL. template.tsx behaves like layout.tsx but re-mounts on every navigation instead of persisting, so use it only when a segment must reset state or replay an enter animation on each visit.

Layouts nest by folder depth; the page is the deepest node. A folder with no page.tsx is not routable — it only contributes a layout to its children.

app-router-model.text: The App Router turns the app/ folder tree directly into your route table — there is no separate routes file. A folder is a URL segment. A segment becomes an addressable page only when it contains a page.tsx; otherwise the folder just holds shared files or a layout for its children. Special files attach to a segment and cascade to every nested segment: layout.tsx renders a persistent shell around its subtree (the root app/layout.tsx is mandatory and defines <html>/<body>), loading.tsx is the Suspense fallback shown while that segment streams, error.tsx is a Client Component error boundary that catches errors thrown while rendering that segment's page and anything nested below it — server or client errors alike — but NOT an error thrown by the segment's own layout.tsx (that is caught by the parent segment's error.tsx, or app/global-error.tsx for the root layout), and not-found.tsx handles misses. Rendering a URL is a two-part walk: find the deepest folder with a page (that is your leaf), then wrap it in every layout from the root down, outermost to innermost. Two folder tricks change the URL shape without new segments: route groups (folder) let you scope a layout to some routes without adding to the path, and dynamic segments [id] capture a path piece as a param. Once you see the tree as "layouts wrap the matched page, top-down," every "which header is showing / why did this 404" question becomes a lookup, not a guess.

server-vs-client-components.proof: A boundary classifier that labels a component server or client from its features and flags a secret imported across the "use client" boundary.
server-vs-client-components.unlock: You can state the rules that force "use client" and explain why anything in a client file (and its imports) ships to the browser.
server-vs-client-components.outcome: Decide correctly whether a component is a Server or Client Component, and catch the two boundary violations: using state/hooks without "use client", and importing a secret into the client graph.
server-vs-client-components.doNotClaim: Don't claim a component is safe because it works locally — a leaked secret in a client file compiles fine and ships to every browser.

server-vs-client-components.text: A component reads process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY to show a price and, because it also used useState, someone slapped "use client" on top. It works — and it just published your Stripe secret to the browser bundle. The server/client split is a security boundary, not a performance toggle, and this lesson makes the rules mechanical so a violation is caught in review, not in a breach.

In the App Router, components are Server Components by DEFAULT: they render on the server, can fetch data and read secrets, and add zero JavaScript to the client bundle — but they cannot use state, effects, or browser APIs. Adding the "use client" directive at the top of a file (before imports) marks a boundary: that component, its helpers, and ALL its imports become part of the client bundle shipped to the browser. So interactivity (useState, onClick, useEffect) forces "use client"; and anything a client file imports — including a module that reads a secret — travels to the browser too.

server-vs-client-components.prompt: Before reading: a component uses useState AND reads process.env.DATABASE_URL. Can it be a single component? What has to change?
server-vs-client-components.reveal: No — not safely. useState forces "use client", but a client component's code (and imports) ship to the browser, so reading DATABASE_URL there would expose the secret. Split it: a Server Component reads the secret and does the data work, then passes only the safe, serializable result as a prop to a small Client Component that owns the useState. The secret never crosses the boundary.

Instead, keep the component on the server and extract only the interactive part into a small client child.

server-vs-client-components.text: Server Components are the default and they run only on the server: they can await a database, read process.env secrets, and render HTML while contributing nothing to the client JavaScript bundle. Their cost is that they have no interactivity — no useState, useEffect, event handlers, or window/document. To get interactivity you add the "use client" directive at the very top of a file (before any import). That directive draws a boundary: the marked component, its local helpers and variables, AND every module it imports are compiled into the client bundle and shipped to the browser. Two rules fall out. First, interactivity forces "use client" — if a component needs state or an onClick, it (or a child) must be a Client Component. Second, the client is untrusted — anything reachable from a "use client" file reaches the browser, so a module that reads a secret must never be imported into that graph. The correct pattern is to push the boundary DOWN: do the secret work and data fetching in a Server Component, then pass only serializable, non-sensitive props into a small Client Component that owns the interactivity. Getting this wrong does not error — it compiles and leaks — which is exactly why you classify components deliberately.

layouts-loading-error.proof: A UI-state resolver that, given a segment's available special files and a render outcome (pending / thrown / ok), returns which special file renders.
layouts-loading-error.unlock: You can predict, for a segment in a given state, whether the user sees the loading, error, not-found, or page UI.
layouts-loading-error.outcome: Use the segment special files correctly: layout.tsx (persistent shell), loading.tsx (Suspense fallback), error.tsx (Client error boundary), not-found.tsx — and know which errors each one actually catches.
layouts-loading-error.doNotClaim: Don't claim error.tsx catches everything — it is a Client boundary that misses the root layout's own errors and catches Server Component errors only via the RSC payload.

layouts-loading-error.text: A slow query makes a page hang with a blank screen, and when it eventually throws, the whole app crashes to a white page instead of showing a scoped error. The team never added the segment files that turn these states into UI. Loading and error are not afterthoughts — they are files with precise semantics, and this lesson pins down exactly which file handles which state.

Each route segment can declare special files that Next wires into the React tree automatically. layout.tsx is a persistent shell that does NOT re-render on navigation within its subtree. loading.tsx is rendered as a Suspense fallback while that segment (and its data) stream in. error.tsx is a Client Component error boundary ("use client" is required) that catches errors thrown while rendering that segment — including Server Component errors, which are surfaced to it through the RSC payload. not-found.tsx renders when notFound() is called. Crucially, error.tsx does NOT catch errors in the SAME segment's layout.tsx (those bubble to the parent) — so the root layout needs global-error.tsx.

layouts-loading-error.prompt: Before reading: a Server Component in app/reports/page.tsx throws while fetching. Which file renders the error UI — and does app/reports/error.tsx catch it or does it bubble up?
layouts-loading-error.reveal: app/reports/error.tsx catches it. Even though the error originates in a Server Component, Next surfaces it to the nearest error.tsx boundary via the RSC payload, and error.tsx (a Client Component) renders the fallback with a reset() to retry. The exception: if the error is thrown in that segment's OWN layout.tsx, error.tsx cannot catch its own boundary's parent — it bubbles to the parent segment's error boundary (and the root layout needs global-error.tsx).

layouts-loading-error.intro: The special files of one segment and the state each one owns.
steps: layout.tsx is a persistent shell — it stays mounted across navigations within its subtree.
loading.tsx shows automatically while the segment and its async data resolve (a Suspense fallback).
error.tsx is a Client boundary; it catches this segment's render errors, including Server Component errors via the RSC payload.
A segment's own layout error is NOT caught by its own error.tsx — it bubbles up; the root uses global-error.tsx.
layouts-loading-error.commonMistake: Forgetting "use client" on error.tsx. Error boundaries rely on client-side lifecycle (getDerivedStateFromError runs during client render), so an error.tsx without the directive is invalid and the error escapes to a parent — often blanking a larger part of the app than intended.

layouts-loading-error.text: The App Router lets each segment declare files that React wires in automatically, and each one owns a specific render state. layout.tsx is the persistent wrapper for a segment and everything nested below it; it renders once and stays mounted across navigations inside its subtree, which is why shared chrome (nav, sidebars) lives there rather than in a page. loading.tsx is a Suspense fallback: while the segment's page and its awaited data are still resolving, Next streams this file to the browser first, so the user sees a skeleton instead of a blank frame. error.tsx is a React error boundary and MUST be a Client Component — its getDerivedStateFromError runs during client rendering — and it catches errors thrown while rendering ITS segment, including errors thrown inside Server Components (those are intercepted server-side and delivered to the boundary through the RSC payload, not by throwing on the client). It receives { error, reset } so the user can retry. The one gap to remember: a boundary cannot catch an error in its own segment's layout.tsx (that layout is above the boundary), so such errors bubble to the parent, and the root layout is protected by global-error.tsx instead. not-found.tsx renders when your code calls notFound(). Learn the state→file map and "blank screen / white crash" stops being mysterious.

data-fetching-server-components.text: A dashboard takes 1.8 seconds to render. Three independent Server Component fetches each take ~600ms and they run one after another because each is on its own await line. The data is not even related. This is a request waterfall, and it is invisible until you measure it. This lesson makes fetch timing and caching something you plan, not something you discover in production traces.

A Server Component can be an async function and await data directly — no useEffect, no client fetch, no loading state plumbing. Next extends fetch with caching controls: by default many fetches are cached, fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" }) opts out for always-fresh data, and { next: { revalidate: N } } serves cached data and refreshes it every N seconds (Incremental Static Regeneration / time-based revalidation). The performance trap is the WATERFALL: if you await three independent fetches on three sequential lines, their times ADD. Independent fetches should run in parallel (start them all, then await together) so the total is the MAX, not the SUM.

Parallel: max(300, 500, 200) = 500ms — you start all three, then await them together (e.g. Promise.all), so they overlap and the total is the slowest one. Since the data is independent, sequential awaiting wastes 500ms for nothing.

steps: A Server Component can be async and await data directly — no client fetch, no effect.
Choose cache per fetch: no-store (always fresh), revalidate:N (refresh every N seconds), force-cache (static).

data-fetching-server-components.text: Data fetching in the App Router moves into the component: a Server Component can be an async function and simply await its data, so there is no client-side fetch, no useEffect, and no manual loading/error state — the loading.tsx and error.tsx from the previous lesson handle those states for free. Next augments the native fetch with per-call caching, and the mode is a decision you make request by request: cache: "no-store" means always fetch fresh (dynamic data like a user's dashboard), next: { revalidate: N } serves cached data and refreshes it at most every N seconds (time-based revalidation, good for data that can be slightly stale), and cache: "force-cache" makes it effectively static. Two fetches to the same URL with the same options are also deduplicated within a render. The performance discipline is avoiding the request WATERFALL: awaiting independent fetches on separate lines makes their latencies add up, because each await blocks the next. When fetches do not depend on each other, start them all first and await them together (Promise.all), so they overlap and total time collapses to the slowest one. Reserve sequential awaits for genuinely dependent data — where the second fetch needs the first's result. Cache mode controls freshness; parallelization controls latency; you tune them separately.

A Server Action is a real HTTP endpoint the moment it exists; the form is just one caller. This lesson makes the action a validating boundary, not a convenience wrapper.

A Server Action is an async function marked with the "use server" directive; Next compiles it into a callable server endpoint and lets you pass it straight to a <form action={fn}>. When the form submits, the function runs on the server with a FormData argument — no fetch, no API route to hand-write. Inside, you validate the FormData (it is untrusted user input), perform the mutation (DB write, etc.), and typically call revalidatePath/revalidateTag so the UI refreshes. Because the action is reachable as an endpoint, the security rule is the same as any handler: never trust the input; re-check auth and validate every field server-side.

The Server Action is a public server endpoint: it must independently validate that fields are present, within limits, and that THIS user is allowed to perform the mutation. The form UX is a convenience; the action is the boundary.

server-actions.text: Server Actions collapse the "write an API route, then fetch it from the client" ceremony into a single async function marked "use server". Next compiles that function into a server endpoint and lets you hand it to a form via <form action={createPost}>; on submit, the function executes on the server with the submitted FormData, and the framework wires up the request for you. Inside the action you do three things in order: validate, mutate, revalidate. Validation matters more than it looks, because the action is a genuine public endpoint — the form is only one possible caller, and an attacker can invoke it with arbitrary FormData. So the client-side niceties (required, maxlength) are UX, not security; the action must independently confirm every field is present and within bounds, coerce types explicitly (FormData values are strings or Files), and re-derive the acting user from the trusted server session rather than trusting any id in the payload. After a successful mutation you call revalidatePath or revalidateTag (next lesson) so the cached UI reflects the new state. The mental shift is that a Server Action is not a "form helper" — it is server code at a network boundary, and it earns trust the same way every endpoint does: by validating its input and its caller.

forms-validation.proof: A schema validator that checks a submitted object field-by-field and returns a map of field → error message (empty when valid).

forms-validation.text: A signup form throws a 500 when someone submits an empty email, and when it does save, "  Alice@EXAMPLE.com " and "alice@example.com" become two different accounts. There is no schema — just scattered if-checks — so errors are inconsistent and the UI cannot show which field failed. This lesson turns validation into one schema pass that yields per-field errors.

A robust form validates its input against a SCHEMA (a declarative set of rules per field: required, type, min/max length, format) and returns a structured result: either the parsed value, or a map of field → message. Libraries like Zod express this as z.object({...}) with .safeParse() returning { success, error }. Two steps come BEFORE the rules: coercion (FormData values are strings — convert numbers/booleans) and normalization (trim whitespace, lowercase emails) so "  A@B.com " and "a@b.com" do not diverge. The output shape matters: a field-keyed error map lets the form re-render each input with its own message, instead of one generic failure.

forms-validation.prompt: Before reading: the same email arrives as "  Bob@Site.COM " one day and "bob@site.com" another. What must validation do so they are treated as one identity?
forms-validation.reveal: Normalize before comparing/storing: trim surrounding whitespace and lowercase the email so both inputs become "bob@site.com". Normalization (and type coercion) happen BEFORE the rule checks and before persistence — otherwise you validate and store two "different" values that are really the same identity, creating duplicate accounts and broken lookups.

forms-validation.commonMistake: Checking the format before normalizing — validating "  Alice@EXAMPLE.com " as-is passes a loose regex but stores a mixed-case, space-padded value that will never match "alice@example.com" on lookup. Normalize, then validate, then store the normalized value.

forms-validation.text: Good form handling replaces scattered if-statements with a single schema: a declarative description of each field's rules — required, type, length, range, format — evaluated in one pass that returns a structured result. The result is not a boolean; it is either the clean parsed value or a map from field name to a specific message, because the UI needs to place each error beside its own input, not show one generic "form invalid." Two operations must run before the rules, and their order is the part people get wrong. Coercion converts raw input into the right type: FormData values arrive as strings, so a numeric field needs Number(v) and an explicit Number.isInteger / NaN check, and a checkbox needs a boolean. Normalization canonicalizes equivalent inputs: trim surrounding whitespace, lowercase emails and usernames, collapse repeated spaces — so that "  Bob@Site.COM " and "bob@site.com" become the same value before you check uniqueness or store it. Only after coercing and normalizing do you apply the rules, and you persist the NORMALIZED value, not the raw one. Doing this on the server (in the Server Action) is what makes it a real boundary — client validation is a UX accelerant, but the schema pass on the server is the one that actually protects the data. Zod's z.object(...).safeParse() is the same idea packaged: it coerces, checks, and hands you either data or a field-addressable error tree.

Then we normalize to a canonical form, trimming and lowercasing so " Alice@EXAMPLE.com " and alice@example.com stop becoming two accounts.
Only now do we apply the schema rules: required, type, length, range, and format, all evaluated in one declarative pass.
The schema is the fork: it does not return a boolean, it branches into either failure or a clean parsed value.
If any field fails, we return a field-to-message map, so the UI can place each error beside its own input, not one generic banner.
If all fields pass, we emit the clean typed value, safe to save, no 500s, no duplicate accounts, no scattered if-checks.

optimistic-updates.text: A like button feels instant — until the request fails and the UI is stuck showing a like that never persisted, permanently out of sync with the database. The team applied the change optimistically but never captured a rollback point, so failure leaves a lie on screen. Optimism without rollback is just a bug that usually hides. This lesson makes the full cycle explicit.

An optimistic update shows the expected result immediately, before the server confirms, to remove perceived latency. React exposes useOptimistic for this in Client Components. The discipline is a three-step cycle: (1) SNAPSHOT the current state before touching it, (2) APPLY the optimistic change and fire the mutation, (3) on success RECONCILE with the authoritative server value (which may differ from your guess), or on failure ROLL BACK to the snapshot and surface an error. Skipping the snapshot means you cannot roll back; skipping reconciliation means your optimistic guess silently overrides the truth.

Without the snapshot you only have 6 and no clean way back; you might naively decrement, but that breaks if multiple updates raced. The snapshot taken before the change is the single source of truth for rollback.

optimistic-updates.commonMistake: Rolling back by inverting the operation (e.g. decrementing after a failed increment) instead of restoring a snapshot. Under concurrent updates the inverse is wrong — the only correct rollback is the exact state you captured before applying the change.

optimistic-updates.text: An optimistic update trades certainty for perceived speed: you render the change you EXPECT before the server confirms it, so the interface feels instant. That trade is only safe if you can undo it, which is why optimism is a full cycle, not a single render. Step one is to SNAPSHOT the current state before you mutate anything — this captured value is the sole authoritative rollback point, and it must be taken before the optimistic change so it is uncontaminated. Step two APPLIES the predicted change to the UI and fires the real mutation (a Server Action). Step three has two branches. On success you RECONCILE: the server's response is authoritative and may not equal your guess (it might assign an id, a server timestamp, a de-duplicated count), so you overwrite the optimistic value with the real one rather than assuming you were right. On failure you ROLL BACK to the snapshot exactly — not by inverting the operation, which breaks under concurrency, but by restoring the captured state — and you show an error so the user knows the action did not stick. React's useOptimistic implements this pattern for Client Components: it shows the optimistic value during the pending transition and automatically reverts to the real state when the action resolves. The failure mode to fear is a "successful-looking" optimistic update with no snapshot: it looks great until the network blips, and then the UI is permanently lying about data the server never accepted.

On error you restore the snapshot, undoing the optimistic lie so the UI matches reality again.
The snapshot feeds both branches — that's the insight: optimism without a rollback point is just a lie waiting to stick.

revalidation-caching.text: A user edits a product; the product page updates, but the homepage carousel and the category listing still show the old name for a minute, because only the edited route was revalidated. Cache invalidation is the classic hard problem, and Next gives you two precise tools — by path and by tag. This lesson makes "what did my mutation just make stale" a computation, not a hope.

Next caches fetched data, and after a mutation you must invalidate the cache so stale data is not served. Two APIs: revalidatePath("/products/42") invalidates the cached data for a specific ROUTE (and its layout). revalidateTag("products") invalidates every fetch that opted into that TAG via fetch(url, { next: { tags: ["products"] } }) — regardless of which route it appears on. Path-based is precise when the change affects one URL; tag-based is right when the same data appears across MANY routes (a product name in a page, a carousel, and a listing all tagged "products"). Choosing wrong leaves some surface stale.

The name is shared data appearing on many routes, so the right tool is revalidateTag("products"), where all three fetches opted into the "products" tag. Tag-based invalidation refreshes every place that data appears, independent of route; path-based refreshes one URL.

revalidation-caching.commonMistake: Calling only revalidatePath for data that appears on multiple routes. The edited route refreshes and looks correct, so the bug hides — but every other route showing that data serves the stale cached copy until it independently expires.

revalidation-caching.text: Caching makes reads fast; the hard part is invalidation — making sure a mutation does not leave stale data being served. Next gives two surgical tools, and choosing between them is about the SHAPE of what changed. revalidatePath(route) invalidates the cached render/data for a specific URL (and the layout that wraps it); it is exactly right when a mutation affects one page and only that page. revalidateTag(tag) is the more powerful one: any fetch can opt into one or more cache tags via fetch(url, { next: { tags: ["products"] } }), and calling revalidateTag("products") invalidates EVERY tagged fetch with that tag no matter which route renders it. That is what you want when the same underlying data appears in several places — a product name shown on its detail page, a homepage carousel, and a category listing. Path invalidation would refresh only one of those and silently leave the others stale; tag invalidation refreshes all of them because they share the tag. The practical rule: tag your fetches by the DATA they represent (an entity type like "products", or a specific entity like "product:42"), then after a mutation invalidate the narrowest tag that covers everywhere the changed data appears. Reserve revalidatePath for genuinely route-local changes. This is the cache-layer version of the reconciliation instinct from optimistic updates: after a write, actively make every cached surface agree with the database instead of waiting for time-based expiry to eventually catch up.

The core lesson: use path when a change affects one page; use tags when shared data appears across many routes.

supabase-client-setup.text: A developer wants an admin dashboard to "just see everything," so they initialize the browser Supabase client with the service_role key. Every query now bypasses Row-Level Security, and the key is sitting in the client bundle — a full-database read/write handed to anyone who opens dev tools. Which key runs where is the whole security model. This lesson makes the pairing a rule you enforce, not a convenience you reach for.

Supabase gives your project two keys. The anon (publishable) key is safe for the browser: it identifies the project and, combined with the user's auth token, executes queries UNDER that user's Row-Level Security policies. The service_role key BYPASSES RLS entirely and must live only in trusted server code (server components, server actions, edge functions) — never in the browser, never in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable. In Next.js you create context-appropriate clients: a browser client (anon key), a server client that reads the user's cookies (anon key, still RLS-bound to that user), and — rarely — an admin client with the service_role key for privileged server-only tasks.

The service_role key bypasses RLS, so exposing it in the client would let anyone read/write the entire database. Privileged work stays server-side behind the same boundary as any secret.

supabase-client-setup.text: A Supabase project exposes two keys with fundamentally different authority, and safe setup is about pairing each with the right execution context. The anon (publishable) key is designed to be public: it identifies your project and, when combined with a signed-in user's JWT, runs every query UNDER that user's Row-Level Security policies — so even though the key is in the browser, the user can only touch rows the database permits. The service_role key is the opposite: it BYPASSES RLS completely, acting as a superuser over your data, which is exactly why it must never appear in the browser, in client-bundled code, or in any NEXT_PUBLIC_ environment variable. In a Next.js app you therefore create context-specific clients: a browser client (anon key) for Client Components, a server client (anon key plus the request's auth cookies) for Server Components and Server Actions — still fully RLS-bound to the requesting user — and, only when you have a genuine administrative need, a server-only admin client with the service_role key. The trap is treating the service_role key as a shortcut when RLS blocks a query; that does not fix authorization, it deletes it. The discipline is the same secret-boundary rule from the server/client lesson, now applied to database keys: the powerful key stays server-side, the browser only ever gets the RLS-respecting one, and "which key runs where" is a property you can verify, not a hope.

postgres-schema-basics.text: A todos table has no primary key, stores user as free-text email, and lets title be null. Duplicate rows pile up, a user renames their email and orphans their data, and RLS has nothing to key on because there is no stable owner column. The schema is where correctness is cheapest to enforce. This lesson makes constraints and the owner column deliberate, so bad data cannot exist and authorization has a hook.

A Postgres table earns its keep through constraints. A PRIMARY KEY gives every row a stable unique identity (commonly a uuid default gen_random_uuid()). A FOREIGN KEY ties a row to its parent (e.g. user_id uuid references auth.users) and can specify referential actions like on delete cascade. NOT NULL forbids missing required values; UNIQUE forbids duplicates (e.g. a username). For a Supabase app, the load-bearing column is user_id referencing auth.users(id): it records who OWNS each row, and it is exactly the column every Row-Level Security policy will compare against auth.uid(). No owner column, no per-user authorization.

  id         uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),   -- stable identity
  user_id    uuid not null references auth.users (id)       -- OWNER: the RLS hook

  title      text not null,                                 -- required
  done       boolean not null default false,
  slug       text unique,                                   -- no duplicate slugs
  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

postgres-schema-basics.text: A relational schema is not just storage shape — it is a set of guarantees the database enforces so your application code does not have to. Four constraints carry most of the weight. A PRIMARY KEY gives each row a unique, stable identity; a surrogate uuid with default gen_random_uuid() is the common choice in Supabase because it is opaque and collision-free. A FOREIGN KEY declares that a value must reference an existing row in another table, and its referential actions decide what happens to children when a parent changes — on delete cascade removes dependents, on delete restrict blocks the delete, on delete set null orphans them intentionally. NOT NULL forbids missing required values, turning "we assumed title was always present" into a guarantee. UNIQUE forbids duplicates on columns that must be one-per-value, like a username or slug. Together these make invalid states unrepresentable, which is far cheaper than catching them in application code after they occur. For a Supabase app there is one column that is special: an owner reference, user_id uuid references auth.users(id), stamped with the creator's id. It is special because it is the exact column Row-Level Security keys on — every "users can only see/modify their own rows" policy compares auth.uid() to this column. Store ownership as this immutable FK, never as mutable free text like an email, or authorization loses its anchor the first time a user changes that value.

ssr-auth-sessions.proof: An auth-decision function that authorizes a protected action only when the identity came from a server-validated source, and rejects a session-only (cookie-read) identity.
ssr-auth-sessions.unlock: You can explain why getSession() is not safe for authorization and getUser()/getClaims() are.
ssr-auth-sessions.outcome: Verify a user server-side the safe way: use getUser()/getClaims() (server-validated) for authorization decisions, and never trust the user object from getSession() for them.

ssr-auth-sessions.text: A server component gates an admin page on getSession()?.user, and a forged/expired cookie sails right through, because getSession just READS the cookie without validating it. The whole point of server-side auth is that the server does not take the client's word for who they are. This lesson fixes the exact method you call so a protected route is actually protected.

Supabase stores the auth session in cookies so a server can identify the user on each request. But the methods differ in trust. getSession() returns the session from the cookie WITHOUT contacting the auth server — fast, but the user object is only as trustworthy as the cookie, so it must not drive authorization. getUser() calls the Auth server to return the canonical, validated user. getClaims() validates the JWT signature locally against the project's signing keys — fast AND trustworthy — and is the recommended choice for protecting pages and data. Rule: verify identity with getClaims()/getUser() for any authorization decision; use getSession() only when you need the raw token, not for "is this user allowed."

To actually validate, call getClaims() (verifies the JWT signature against the project keys) or getUser() (asks the Auth server) — those confirm the identity is real before you authorize. getSession is for retrieving the token, not for gating access.

That user is a cookie read with no server validation, so an expired or forged cookie authorizes an attacker — always verify with getClaims()/getUser() for access decisions.

ssr-auth-sessions.text: Server-side auth exists so the server does not trust the client's claim about who they are — and that trust distinction is encoded in which Supabase method you call. The session lives in cookies, and getSession() simply reads and returns it WITHOUT any server-side validation: it is fine for grabbing the raw access/refresh token, but the user object it hands back is exactly as trustworthy as the cookie, which is to say not at all for authorization. Two methods give you a validated identity instead. getUser() makes a request to the Supabase Auth server and returns the canonical, server-verified user — authoritative, and what you want when you need the current record (e.g. right after a password change). getClaims() validates the JWT's signature locally against your project's asymmetric signing keys, so it confirms the token is genuine and unexpired WITHOUT a network round-trip — fast enough to run on every request, which is why it is the recommended choice for protecting pages and data. The practical rule is a single sentence: use getClaims()/getUser() to decide "is this user allowed," and use getSession() only when you literally need the token. There is also a Next.js middleware subtlety from the docs — do not run code between createServerClient and auth.getUser(), and always return the response object carrying the refreshed cookies, or the server and browser sessions drift and users get logged out. But the load-bearing fact is the trust one: a protected route validated with getSession is not protected at all.

row-level-security.proof: An RLS policy evaluator that, given a policy predicate, the current user, and a set of rows, computes exactly which rows are visible — the database's authorization decision, in code.
row-level-security.unlock: You can write a per-user SELECT policy and explain why enabling RLS without a policy denies ALL rows.
row-level-security.outcome: Enforce authorization in the database with RLS: enable it per table, write a USING policy (auth.uid() = user_id) that filters reads, and evaluate which rows a given user can see.
row-level-security.doNotClaim: Don't claim a table is secure because your queries filter by user in the app — app-side filtering is bypassable; RLS is the boundary the database itself enforces.

row-level-security.text: A .from("todos").select() in the app filters by the current user in JavaScript — until someone removes the filter, or hits the table from another client, and reads everyone's rows. Authorization written in application code is a suggestion; Row-Level Security is enforcement the database applies to EVERY query. This lesson makes RLS the real boundary by turning a policy into a predicate you can evaluate row by row.

Row-Level Security is Postgres authorization applied per row, per query, by the database itself. You alter table X enable row level security (which, on its own, DENIES all access until a policy grants some), then create policies. A SELECT/DELETE policy has a USING expression evaluated against each EXISTING row — using (auth.uid() = user_id) means "a row is visible only if its user_id equals the current user." INSERT policies use WITH CHECK against the NEW row; UPDATE can use both (USING on the old row, WITH CHECK on the new). auth.uid() is the validated current user's id from the JWT. Because RLS runs in the database, it protects the table no matter which client or code path issues the query — unlike app-side filtering.

row-level-security.prompt: Before reading: you run `alter table todos enable row level security;` and write NO policies. What can a normal user now select from todos?
row-level-security.reveal: Nothing — zero rows. Enabling RLS flips the table to deny-by-default: with no policy granting access, every row is hidden from non-privileged roles. Access is only restored by a policy whose USING expression evaluates true for a row. This is the safe default: you must explicitly grant visibility (e.g. using (auth.uid() = user_id)) rather than accidentally leaving a table open.

row-level-security.code:
-- 1. Turn on RLS (now DENIES everything until a policy grants access)
alter table todos enable row level security;

-- 2. SELECT policy: a row is visible only if the current user owns it.
create policy "own todos are readable"
  on todos for select
  to authenticated
  using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );       -- evaluated per existing row

-- 3. INSERT policy: the NEW row must be owned by the inserter.
create policy "insert own todos"
  on todos for insert
  to authenticated
  with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );  -- evaluated against the NEW row

-- (select auth.uid()) is the validated current user's id (from the JWT). Wrapping it
-- in a subquery lets Postgres evaluate it once per query (an initPlan) instead of once
-- per row; `to authenticated` keeps the policy from running for anonymous requests.
row-level-security.intro: Enable RLS and write the per-user SELECT policy the database enforces.
steps: enable row level security flips the table to deny-by-default — no policy means no rows.
A SELECT policy's USING predicate is evaluated per existing row; true = visible.
using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id) grants each user visibility of only their own rows — the subquery form runs the id lookup once per query, not once per row.
to authenticated scopes the policy to signed-in requests; INSERT uses WITH CHECK on the NEW row so users cannot create rows owned by someone else.
row-level-security.commonMistake: Filtering by user only in the app query (.eq("user_id", currentUser)) and never enabling RLS. The moment any code path drops that filter — or a different client queries the table — every row leaks. RLS enforces the rule in the database so no query can escape it.

row-level-security.text: Row-Level Security moves authorization out of application code and into the database, where it cannot be bypassed. You enable it per table with alter table X enable row level security, and the first crucial fact is that this alone denies everything: with RLS on and no policies, non-privileged roles see zero rows. Access is granted only by policies, and each policy is a boolean expression the database evaluates for every affected row on every query. The command a policy targets determines which expression it uses: SELECT and DELETE policies use a USING clause evaluated against EXISTING rows (does this row satisfy the predicate for this user?); INSERT policies use WITH CHECK evaluated against the NEW row (is the user allowed to create this specific row?); UPDATE policies can use both — USING to decide which rows may be updated and WITH CHECK to constrain what they may be changed into. The canonical per-user predicate is auth.uid() = user_id, where auth.uid() returns the validated current user's id from the JWT and user_id is the owner column from the schema lesson — so a row is visible/mutable only by its owner. Because this runs inside Postgres, it protects the table uniformly: every client, every code path, the browser, a server action, a raw SQL console — all are subject to the same policy. That is why RLS, not app-side .eq() filtering, is the real authorization boundary. Two production refinements matter. First, wrap the call as (select auth.uid()): Postgres then evaluates it once per query as an initPlan and reuses the result for every row, instead of calling the function on each row — on a large table that difference is dramatic, and Supabase’s RLS performance guidance recommends the wrapped form as the default. Second, scope the policy with to authenticated so it never runs for anonymous requests. (No null guard is needed: if auth.uid() is null, null = user_id evaluates to NULL, and RLS treats any non-true predicate as false — the row is simply hidden, so the policy already fails closed.) Get RLS right and "who can see this row" is answered once, in the one place no query can route around.

storyboard.say: A client fires a broad query: select * from todos. It asks for every row in the table, no filter attached.
With RLS enabled, the database runs each todos row through a policy before returning it. Every single row gets checked.
The policy needs to know who is asking. auth.uid() supplies the current user's id into the USING expression.
For each row the database evaluates USING (auth.uid() = user_id) — a boolean verdict per row, deny by default.
Rows the user owns evaluate true, so the policy keeps them. These are the only rows that survive.
Rows belonging to others evaluate false and are silently filtered out — they never leave the database.
Only the owned rows flow into the result set the client receives, no matter how the query was written.
The insight: authorization lives in the database, not the app. Remove the JS filter and the policy still enforces ownership.

reads-under-rls.text: A developer's query returns an empty array for user B even though the table has thousands of rows, and — panicking — they swap in the service_role key to "make it work." Now the query returns everyone's data and the RLS boundary is gone. RLS filtering is SILENT: it removes unauthorized rows without an error, which looks like a bug but is the security model working. This lesson teaches you to read correctly under RLS instead of disabling it.

When RLS is enabled, a SELECT does not error on rows you cannot see — it silently OMITS them. So a query that would return 1000 rows without RLS returns only the caller's rows with it, and if the caller owns none, it returns an empty array with no error. This is correct: the database applied the USING predicate per row. Two consequences for reading: (1) treat an empty/short result as a possible authorization outcome, not automatically a failure — check whether the user should have rows; (2) still select only the columns you need (a projection), because RLS controls WHICH ROWS you get, not which columns — narrow selects reduce payload and avoid leaking unneeded fields.

reads-under-rls.prompt: Before reading: with RLS on, user B (who owns no todos) runs select * from todos. Do they get an error, and how many rows?
reads-under-rls.reveal: No error, zero rows. RLS filters silently: every row fails the USING (auth.uid() = user_id) predicate for user B, so all are omitted and the result is an empty array — a successful query with no matching rows. This is the correct secure behavior; treating the empty result as a failure (and reaching for service_role) would destroy the boundary that is working exactly as designed.

reads-under-rls.text: Reading under RLS changes what "success" looks like. When RLS is enabled, the database evaluates the SELECT policy's USING predicate against every candidate row and simply OMITS the ones that fail — it does not raise an error for rows you are not allowed to see. So the same query that returns thousands of rows as a superuser returns only the caller's permitted rows as a normal user, and if the caller is entitled to none, it returns an empty array with error null. That silence is the single most confusing thing about RLS in practice: an empty or unexpectedly short result is frequently not a bug but the authorization boundary doing its job, and the correct response is to verify the user's identity and the policy predicate, never to reach for the service_role key (which would delete the boundary rather than debug it). Two further habits make RLS reads clean. First, keep authorization and projection distinct in your head: RLS decides WHICH ROWS you receive, while the select() projection decides WHICH COLUMNS — you still narrow columns to what you need, both to shrink payloads and to avoid surfacing fields the feature does not use. Second, remember that RLS-filtered reads are still just fetches, so the parallelization lesson applies — multiple independent RLS-scoped queries on a page should run together, not in a waterfall. Read correctly and RLS is invisible in the happy path and unbypassable in the adversarial one.

writes-transactions.proof: A write evaluator that applies WITH CHECK to an insert/update (allow or reject) AND models a multi-step transaction that rolls back entirely if any step fails.
writes-transactions.unlock: You can explain why a bad write is rejected while a bad read is silently filtered, and why partial multi-step writes must roll back.
writes-transactions.outcome: Write safely under RLS and atomically: understand that INSERT/UPDATE are checked by WITH CHECK (a write violating ownership is REJECTED, not silently dropped), and wrap multi-step writes in a transaction so they all commit or all roll back.

writes-transactions.text: A "transfer" writes a debit to one row and a credit to another as two separate statements; the credit fails, and now money vanished — the debit committed alone. Meanwhile an attacker tries to INSERT a row owned by someone else and expects it to slip through like a filtered read. Writes behave differently from reads under RLS, and multi-step writes need atomicity. This lesson pins down both: WITH CHECK rejection and transactional all-or-nothing.

Writes under RLS use WITH CHECK, not USING. An INSERT policy's WITH CHECK is evaluated against the NEW row and, if it fails, the write is REJECTED with an error — unlike a read, which silently omits. (An UPDATE policy can pair USING on the existing row with WITH CHECK on the resulting row.) Separately, multi-statement writes need ATOMICITY: a transaction (begin … commit, or a single Postgres function / RPC) makes all steps succeed together or roll back together, so a failure midway leaves NO partial state. In Supabase you get atomicity by putting the steps in a database function (an RPC) or a transaction, not by firing independent statements from the client.

writes-transactions.prompt: Before reading: a user tries to INSERT a todo with user_id set to ANOTHER user's id, under an INSERT policy with check (auth.uid() = user_id). Does it silently drop like a filtered read, or error?
writes-transactions.reveal: It ERRORS — the write is rejected. WITH CHECK evaluates the NEW row; since auth.uid() (the inserter) does not equal the user_id they set, the check fails and the INSERT is refused with a policy violation. Writes are rejected loudly, unlike reads which silently omit unauthorized rows. This asymmetry is intentional: you cannot smuggle in a row you are not allowed to create.

writes-transactions.code:
-- INSERT policy: the NEW row must be owned by the inserter, or the write is REJECTED.
create policy "insert own" on todos for insert
  to authenticated
  with check ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );

-- Multi-step change must be ATOMIC — do it in a function (RPC), not two client calls:
create function transfer(from_id uuid, to_id uuid, amount int)
returns void language plpgsql as $$
begin
  update accounts set balance = balance - amount where id = from_id;  -- step 1
  update accounts set balance = balance + amount where id = to_id;    -- step 2
  -- if EITHER update fails, the whole function's transaction ROLLS BACK: no partial write
end; $$;

steps: INSERT/UPDATE authorization uses WITH CHECK on the NEW row; a violating write is rejected with an error.
This is the opposite of reads: bad writes error loudly, bad reads are silently filtered.

writes-transactions.commonMistake: Doing a multi-step change as two separate client calls (debit, then credit). If the second fails, the first has already committed — money or state is now inconsistent. Wrap the steps in one transaction/RPC so a mid-way failure rolls everything back.

writes-transactions.text: Writing under RLS is governed by a different clause than reading, and the behavioral difference matters. A SELECT policy uses USING and silently omits rows you cannot see; an INSERT policy uses WITH CHECK, evaluated against the NEW row you are trying to create, and if it fails the database REJECTS the write with an explicit policy-violation error. (UPDATE sits in between: it can use USING to decide which existing rows you may target and WITH CHECK to constrain what the updated row is allowed to become.) That asymmetry — reads filter quietly, writes fail loudly — is deliberate: you should never be able to smuggle in or mutate a row you are not authorized for, so the attempt is refused rather than silently ignored. The second pillar of safe writes is ATOMICITY. Any change that spans multiple statements — debit one account and credit another, insert a parent then its children, decrement inventory then record an order — must be transactional: begin, do all steps, commit; and if any step fails, the entire unit rolls back so the database is never left in a half-written, inconsistent state. Firing those steps as independent client calls is the classic bug, because a failure after the first call leaves committed partial state with no automatic undo. In Supabase the reliable way to get atomicity is to move the multi-step logic into a Postgres function you invoke as an RPC (or an explicit transaction), so all statements share one transaction boundary. Correct writes therefore satisfy two invariants at once: authorized (WITH CHECK passes) and atomic (all-or-nothing).

storyboard.say: A write begins: an INSERT or a multi-step operation like a transfer that must debit one row and credit another.
Every write is authorized by WITH CHECK, which evaluates the NEW row you are trying to create — not the rows you can read.
If the new row breaks policy — say an attacker inserts a row owned by someone else — the write fails loudly with a policy violation error.
Unlike a read that silently omits rows, a rejected write returns an explicit error, so nothing unauthorized slips through.
When the new row passes the check, the operation enters a transaction — a begin-commit block or a single Postgres function.
If every step succeeds, the transaction commits, and the debit and credit land together as one atomic unit.
If any step fails, the transaction rolls back — the debit is undone too, so money never vanishes into a half-finished write.
The lesson: reads filter quietly, but writes fail loudly under WITH CHECK, and transactions make multi-step writes all-or-nothing.

realtime.proof: A realtime authorization simulator that decides, at channel-join time, whether a user may subscribe to a topic and which change events they then receive under RLS.
realtime.unlock: You can explain when Realtime authorization is evaluated (at connect/join, then cached) and why it means you cannot receive events for rows you cannot read.
realtime.outcome: Subscribe to database changes over a channel and understand that Realtime access is authorized by RLS at CONNECT time (per channel/topic), cached for the connection — so a client only receives change events for rows it is allowed to see.
realtime.doNotClaim: Don't claim Realtime is secure because the UI hides other users' data — security comes from RLS deciding the subscription at connect time, not from client-side filtering of events.

realtime.text: A team builds a live board and filters incoming realtime events in the browser to "only show mine" — but the events for everyone's rows are still streaming to every client, visible in the network tab. Realtime authorization is not a UI concern; Supabase evaluates RLS when the channel connects and only delivers permitted events. This lesson makes the connect-time authorization model explicit so you subscribe securely instead of filtering after the fact.

Supabase Realtime pushes database changes (and broadcast/presence messages) to subscribed clients over a WebSocket channel identified by a topic. Access is controlled by RLS policies on the realtime.messages table: when the client CONNECTS and JOINS a channel topic, Supabase calculates permissions from the RLS policies, the user's auth JWT, the request, and the topic — and CACHES that decision for the duration of the connection (the database is not queried per message). The consequence: a user can only subscribe to topics they are authorized for, and for Postgres change events, they receive changes only for rows their RLS lets them read. Authorization happens once, at join time, not per event and not in the browser.

realtime.prompt: Before reading: when exactly does Supabase check whether a user is allowed on a realtime channel — on every message, or once?
realtime.reveal: Once, at connect/join time. When the WebSocket connects and the client joins a channel topic, Supabase evaluates the RLS policies (on realtime.messages) together with the user's JWT and the topic, then CACHES that authorization for the whole connection — it does not re-query the database per message. So permission is decided up front; if you are not authorized for the topic, you never join it, and you only receive events for rows RLS permits.

realtime.intro: Subscribe to a channel; authorization is decided when you join, under RLS.
steps: A channel has a topic; the client must be authorized to JOIN that topic.
Authorization is RLS-based, evaluated at connect/join time and cached for the connection.
For Postgres change events you only receive changes for rows your RLS permits.
Security is the connect-time decision, not client-side filtering of received events.
realtime.commonMistake: Subscribing broadly and filtering the incoming events in the browser to hide other users' data. The unauthorized events were still transmitted to the client — the fix is authorizing the subscription via RLS at connect time so those events are never sent, not hiding them after arrival.

realtime.text: Realtime turns your database into a push system: subscribed clients receive Postgres change events (inserts/updates/deletes) and broadcast/presence messages over a WebSocket channel identified by a topic. The security model is the part people misplace into the UI, so make it precise: access is governed by Row-Level Security policies on the realtime.messages table, and the crucial timing is that authorization is calculated when the client CONNECTS and JOINS a channel topic — from the RLS policies, the user's auth JWT, the request headers, and the topic being joined — and then CACHED for the duration of that connection. The database is NOT consulted on every message, which is what makes Realtime scale, and it means the authorization decision is made once, up front, per connection. Two consequences follow. First, a client can only subscribe to topics it is permitted to join; an unauthorized join simply does not succeed, so events for that topic are never delivered to it. Second, for Postgres change subscriptions, the same RLS that governs reads governs which change events you receive — you get change notifications only for rows you are allowed to read, so you cannot eavesdrop on other users' data by listening. This is why filtering events in the browser is the wrong mental model: by the time an event reaches a correctly-configured client, RLS already decided it was allowed to have it. You secure Realtime by writing the RLS policies that gate the subscription, not by hiding events after they arrive.

storyboard.say: A client opens a WebSocket and joins a channel topic, asking Supabase Realtime to stream that table's live changes.
At that join, the auth JWT is presented alongside the request — it carries the identity RLS needs to reason about.
RLS on realtime.messages runs now, at connect time, combining the JWT, the request, and the topic into a single yes-or-no decision.
If the policy denies, the join itself fails — an unauthorized client never subscribes to the channel at all.
If authorized, that decision is cached for the whole connection; the database is not re-checked on every message.
Only permitted change events then flow down this authorized channel — the server decides what streams, not the browser.
The insight: filtering in the UI is theater — real security is RLS evaluated at connect and cached, so events for other rows never leave the server.

  with check ( bucket_id = 'avatars'

storage.text: Supabase Storage is not a separate security universe — it is Postgres RLS applied to files. The idiomatic, robust pattern is to encode ownership in the object's PATH: make the first folder segment the owner's user id, so a file is stored as "<uid>/avatar.png", and then write policies that permit access only when the object's bucket_id matches the intended bucket AND the first path segment equals auth.uid(). Buckets also carry a public/private flag, but it is coarse: public means objects are readable by anyone with the URL, private means every access is mediated by policies; either way, WHICH authenticated users may read or write WHICH objects is decided by the storage.objects RLS policies, so a private bucket with no policies is not "secure by default," it is simply inaccessible or misconfigured. This lesson makes route protection precise: a matcher, a session refresh, a redirect — layered on top of RLS, never instead of it.

Next.js middleware runs before a request is completed and can rewrite, redirect, or continue it; you scope it with a matcher config so it runs only on the paths you intend (excluding static assets). The Supabase SSR pattern uses middleware to REFRESH the auth session cookies on each request and to redirect unauthenticated users to /login. middleware-route-protection.text: Next.js middleware executes before a matched request is served and can continue, rewrite, or redirect it, scoped by a matcher config so it runs only where you intend and skips static assets. In a Supabase app it plays a specific, valuable role: on every request it REFRESHES the auth session (keeping the cookies current so the user stays logged in) and it can REDIRECT unauthenticated users away from protected paths to /login. The official pattern has two non-negotiable mechanics: do not insert code between createServerClient and auth.getUser() (a subtle ordering bug there causes random logouts), and always return the response object that carries the refreshed cookies, or the browser and server sessions drift apart and the user is signed out prematurely. But the conceptual point that keeps apps secure is knowing what middleware IS and IS NOT. It is a perimeter that shapes navigation and UX — it makes the logged-out experience correct by bouncing users to login. It is NOT the authoritative data boundary, because plenty of access paths do not traverse a page navigation: a direct call to a data API, a server action invoked out of band, a query from a mobile client or a script. Those must still be stopped by the real boundary, which is Row-Level Security in the database plus server-side identity checks on your endpoints. So middleware and RLS are layered, not alternatives: middleware gives a clean, fast UX gate at the edge, and RLS guarantees that even a request that skips the edge cannot read or write rows it should not. Ship both; rely on RLS for correctness.

env-secrets.proof: An env-var leak detector that flags any NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable holding a secret and any secret read where the client can reach it.
env-secrets.unlock: You can state exactly which env vars ship to the browser and why the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix is a publish decision, not a naming style.
env-secrets.outcome: Classify every environment variable correctly: NEXT_PUBLIC_* is inlined into the browser bundle (never a secret), everything else is server-only — and detect a secret smuggled into a public variable.

env-secrets.text: Someone names a variable NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY so the frontend can read it, and Next dutifully inlines that god-mode key into the JavaScript shipped to every visitor. The prefix is not a convention — it is an instruction to PUBLISH the value to the browser. This lesson makes env classification mechanical: public prefix means public, no exceptions, and a secret behind that prefix is a breach you can detect before deploy.

In Next.js, an environment variable is exposed to the browser ONLY if its name begins with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Such variables are INLINED into the client JavaScript bundle at build time, so they are readable by anyone — they are for non-secret config like a public API URL or the Supabase anon key (which is safe by design, because RLS constrains it). Every other variable (no prefix) is server-only: available in Server Components, Server Actions, route handlers, and middleware, but never sent to the client. The load-bearing rule: the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix is a decision to PUBLISH the value. A true secret (service_role key, a DB URL, a private API key) must never carry it.

The anon key is designed to be public because RLS still constrains every query it makes to the signed-in user's permissions. The service_role key BYPASSES RLS — it is a superuser key — so inlining it into the browser bundle (which is what NEXT_PUBLIC_ does) hands full database control to every visitor. Prefix = publish; only publish values that are safe when public.

The prefix does not grant safe access — it inlines the value into everyone's browser bundle. If the client needs privileged data, fetch it through a server endpoint, do not expose the key.

env-secrets.text: Next.js has one simple, load-bearing rule for environment variables: a variable is exposed to browser code if and only if its name begins with NEXT_PUBLIC_, and any such variable is INLINED into the client JavaScript bundle at build time. "Inlined" is the word that matters — the value is literally baked into the shipped JS, readable by anyone who opens the bundle, cacheable on CDNs, impossible to un-send. So the prefix is not a naming style or a hint; it is a decision to PUBLISH the value to every visitor. That makes classification binary and consequential. Values that are safe when public — a public API base URL, the Supabase project URL, the Supabase anon/publishable key — belong behind NEXT_PUBLIC_. The anon key is the instructive case: it is safe to publish precisely because Row-Level Security constrains every query it issues to the signed-in user's permissions, so exposing it grants no unauthorized power. Everything else — the service_role key (which bypasses RLS), a database connection string, a private third-party API key, any password or signing secret — has NO prefix and stays server-only, reachable from Server Components, Server Actions, route handlers, and middleware but never transmitted to the client. The dangerous move is prefixing a secret "so the client can use it": that does not give the client safe access, it publishes the secret. When the browser genuinely needs privileged data, the answer is to expose a server endpoint that reads the secret and returns only the safe result — the same push-the-boundary-down discipline from the server/client lesson, now applied to configuration. Which vars ship to the browser is something you can audit deterministically, and a secret behind NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a breach you should catch before it deploys.

With the prefix, the value is inlined into the client bundle at build time, baked into shipped JavaScript that anyone can read.
With no prefix, the variable stays in the server-only runtime, never shipped to the browser.
That is why the anon key and project URL are fine in the bundle: they're public by design, constrained by row-level security.
The service_role key and database URL belong on the server only. They must never carry the prefix.
Prefix a secret and Next inlines god-mode credentials into every visitor's JavaScript. Cached, un-sendable, catastrophic.
The rule is binary: NEXT_PUBLIC_ means publish to the world. Classify carefully, because the leak cannot be undone.

Match the exact observable contract, retain a boundary-failure regression, and name the browser, database, RLS, identity, deployment, and production evidence still required. env-secrets.task: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix inlines this secret into the browser. Remove the prefix and access it server-side.
env-secrets.symptom: A private third-party API key is showing up in the browser network tab and in the built JS chunks.

// .env

optionA.text: Keep the key server-only and expose a Server Action / route that uses it and returns only the safe result. The secret never leaves the server; the client gets exactly what it needs.
optionA.label: Server endpoint proxy

optionB.text: Add NEXT_PUBLIC_ so the client reads the key directly. It "works," but it inlines the secret into every browser bundle — a permanent leak that a rotation only temporarily fixes.
optionB.label: Prefix the key

env-secrets.guidance: Add a server endpoint (A). The rule is absolute: never publish a secret to satisfy a client need. Proxy through the server so the key stays server-only and the browser receives just the result. Prefixing a secret (B) is the exact breach this lesson exists to prevent.
env-secrets.question: A client component needs data that requires a private API key. Prefix the key NEXT_PUBLIC_, or add a server endpoint?

options: It restricts the value to server-side code, marking it public API within your own app while keeping it out of anything compiled for the browser bundle.
It marks the variable as required, so the build fails when it is unset — which is how a deploy catches a missing key before the first request lands.
It ships the variable to the client over the encrypted RSC payload at runtime, rather than embedding the literal value inside the built JavaScript chunks.
It inlines the value into the client JS bundle at build time, so anyone can read it — the prefix publishes, and only non-secret values may carry it.
env-secrets.question: What does the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix actually do to a variable?
env-secrets.explanation: NEXT_PUBLIC_ exposes and inlines the value into the browser bundle at build time. It is a publish instruction, not protection, so only values safe to be public (like the anon key or a public URL) may carry it; secrets must have no prefix and stay server-only.

items: Only non-secret values carry the NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.
The service_role key, DB URL, and private keys are server-only (no prefix).
You can detect a secret exposed via a public-prefixed variable before deploy.

deploy-vercel.proof: A deploy-readiness gate that verifies all required env vars are present, none are secrets behind a public prefix, and returns a pass/fail with the exact blocking issues.
deploy-vercel.unlock: You can enumerate the env vars a production deploy needs and gate the deploy on their correct presence and scope.
deploy-vercel.outcome: Ship the app with a correct production configuration: every required env var set in the platform (with the public/server split preserved), and a pre-deploy check that fails the build if a required secret is missing or a secret is exposed.
deploy-vercel.doNotClaim: Don't claim it is production-ready because it builds — a build can succeed while a missing server secret or a leaked public one waits to fail (or breach) at runtime.

deploy-vercel.text: A deploy goes green, then production 500s on the first request because SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY was never set on the platform — it only lived in a local .env. Or worse, it deploys fine because someone made the key NEXT_PUBLIC_ to "get past the error," publishing it. Deploy config is where the whole course's security either holds or leaks. This lesson turns "hope the env is right" into a pre-deploy gate that fails loudly on a missing or leaked variable.

Deploying a Next.js + Supabase app means the code AND its environment must both be correct in production. Env vars set locally in .env do NOT travel to the host — you set them in the platform (e.g. Vercel Project Settings → Environment Variables), preserving the public/server split: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY are public build-time vars, while SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY and any DB/secret stay server-only. Two production failure modes are worth gating: a REQUIRED variable missing (the app 500s at runtime, not at build), and a SECRET exposed via a public prefix (a breach that ships silently). A pre-deploy check that asserts presence and correct scope catches both before they reach users.

deploy-vercel.prompt: Before reading: your app builds and runs locally with a .env file. You deploy and it 500s immediately. What is the most likely cause?
deploy-vercel.reveal: The environment variables were not set on the hosting platform — .env is local and does not deploy. The build can still succeed (it does not need every runtime secret to compile), then the first request fails because, say, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY or DATABASE_URL is undefined in production. You must configure each required var in the platform's environment settings, preserving the public/server split, and ideally gate the deploy on their presence.

deploy-vercel.intro: A pre-deploy gate asserting env presence and correct public/server scope.
steps: Local .env does not deploy — set every required var in the platform's environment settings.
Preserve the split: public NEXT_PUBLIC_* vars vs server-only secrets.
Gate on PRESENCE: a missing required var 500s at runtime, not at build — catch it early.
Gate on SCOPE: fail if any secret sits behind a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.
deploy-vercel.commonMistake: Assuming a green build means a green deploy. The build compiles without every runtime secret, so a missing SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY or DATABASE_URL passes the build and then crashes the first production request — presence must be asserted explicitly, not inferred from a successful build.

deploy-vercel.text: Shipping is not just pushing code; it is ensuring the runtime ENVIRONMENT is correct in production, and that is where a Next.js + Supabase app most often breaks or leaks. The first fact is that a local .env file is local — it is not uploaded to your host — so every variable the app needs at runtime must be configured in the platform's environment settings (on Vercel, Project Settings → Environment Variables), and the public/server distinction from the previous lesson must be preserved there: NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY are public build-time values, while SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, DATABASE_URL, and any private key are server-only. The second fact is that a successful BUILD does not prove a correct environment. The build compiles the app; it does not exercise every runtime secret, so a required server variable can be entirely absent and the build still turns green — then the first production request 500s because that variable is undefined at runtime. That failure is invisible until a user hits it, which is exactly why you add a pre-deploy GATE: a check that runs before (or as part of) the deploy and asserts two things — PRESENCE (every required variable, public and server, is actually set) and SCOPE (no secret is sitting behind a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix, i.e. the env-leak detector from the previous lesson, enforced at ship time). A missing var is a reliability bug; a leaked secret is a security bug; the gate turns both from runtime surprises into a failed, fixable pre-deploy step. Production-ready therefore means: it builds, its environment is fully and correctly configured on the platform, and a gate has proven the presence-and-scope invariants — not merely that the compiler was happy.
deploy-vercel.title: Production readiness is code plus a verified environment, gated before deploy
The pre-deploy gate
deploy-vercel.subtitle: presence + scope must pass before code reaches users

storyboard.say: Deploying means two things must be right at once: the code that builds, and the environment it runs inside on the host.
When your build succeeds, the code is submitted to a pre-deploy gate that decides whether it's safe to reach users.
That gate also checks the platform's environment variables, because a local .env file never travels to production.
First failure: a required server var like SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY is absent, so production 500s on the first request.
Second failure: someone slaps NEXT_PUBLIC_ on a secret to silence the error, publishing that key to every browser.
Only when presence and scope both pass — every var set, none leaked — does the gate release the deploy.
Shipping isn't pushing code; it's proving the runtime environment is correct and the public-server split is preserved.

optionA.text: Assert every required var at deploy/startup and fail fast with a clear message. A misconfiguration is caught before users hit it, and the error names exactly what is missing.
optionA.label: Explicit presence gate

optionB.text: Let the app crash whenever the missing var is first read. No upfront code, but the failure is a runtime 500 in production, possibly on a rarely-hit path discovered by a user days later.
optionB.label: Fail on first use

deploy-vercel.guidance: Add the explicit gate (A). Fail-fast validation converts a latent production 500 into a loud, specific pre-deploy (or boot) error you fix immediately. Relying on first-use (B) means your users are your env-var test suite — exactly the outcome shipping discipline exists to avoid.
deploy-vercel.question: Validate required env vars with a startup/pre-deploy check, or just let missing ones surface when first used?

options: The build reused a stale cached artifact, so a green build proves nothing — redeploying with the build cache cleared is what restores a working runtime.
A NEXT_PUBLIC_ var is missing, and those always fail the build first — so a green build already proves every variable the app reads exists in production.
The .env.local file was never committed, so the platform had nothing to read — commit it so the deployed build ships the same values that work locally.
A required runtime env var was never set on the platform, and the build never exercises it — so gate the deploy on the presence of each required var.
