capstone-rls-crud.proof: A pipeline that runs a create request through validate → RLS authorize → mutate → revalidate → RLS-filtered read, and reports the outcome plus what each stage enforced.
capstone-rls-crud.unlock: You can assemble validation, RLS authorization, revalidation, and RLS-filtered reads into one correct, defensible request path.
capstone-rls-crud.outcome: Compose the whole course into one request path: authenticate the user, run a Server Action that validates input, authorize the write with RLS (WITH CHECK), revalidate the cache, and read back only the user's own rows — proving auth-gated CRUD enforced end to end.
capstone-rls-crud.doNotClaim: Don't claim the app is secure because each piece passed alone — the capstone proves they COMPOSE into one path where a bad request is rejected and a good one is authorized, atomic, and consistent.

capstone-rls-crud.text: Every lesson built one primitive: the server/client boundary, Server Actions, form validation, RLS as the real authorization boundary, WITH CHECK writes, revalidation, RLS-filtered reads. Production needs them working TOGETHER on one request path — a logged-in user creates a row, the input is validated, the write is authorized and atomic, the cache is refreshed, and the read returns only their rows. This capstone wires the primitives into that path and runs a scripted create end to end, proving the whole is correct, not just the parts.

A production CRUD write in Next.js + Supabase is a pipeline, not a single call. It (1) confirms a validated identity (getUser/getClaims), (2) invokes a Server Action that validates the FormData, (3) performs the write which the database authorizes via the RLS WITH CHECK policy (rejecting a row the user may not create), (4) calls revalidatePath/revalidateTag so cached reads refresh, and (5) reads back under the SELECT policy so the user sees only their own rows. Each stage was a lesson; the capstone proves they compose — a request missing auth, or with invalid input, or attempting a foreign-owned write, is stopped at the right stage, and a valid one flows through to a consistent, RLS-filtered result.

capstone-rls-crud.prompt: Before reading: list the stages a single authenticated "create a todo" request passes through in this stack, from identity to the read-back.
capstone-rls-crud.reveal: Validated identity (getUser/getClaims) → Server Action → input validation (schema over FormData) → the write authorized by the RLS WITH CHECK policy (owner must be auth.uid()) → revalidatePath/Tag to refresh caches → an RLS-filtered SELECT read-back returning only the user's rows. The capstone is not new material — it is the correct COMPOSITION of these stages into one path, where the wrong request is rejected at the right stage and the right one ends consistent.

capstone-rls-crud.intro: Trace one create request through all six stages, watching what each stage enforces.
steps: Confirm a validated identity before anything else (no user → reject).
Validate the FormData in the Server Action (bad input → reject with a message).
Authorize the write with the RLS WITH CHECK policy (foreign-owned row → reject).
Mutate, revalidate the cache, then read back under the SELECT policy — user sees only their rows.
capstone-rls-crud.commonMistake: Wiring the pipeline but reading back with the service_role key (or without RLS) so the create "looks successful" — reintroducing the exact leak the RLS lessons killed. The read-back must run under the user's SELECT policy, or the app proves nothing about isolation.

capstone-rls-crud.text: The capstone is where the course stops being a list of techniques and becomes one coherent request path, and the discipline is COMPOSITION: each stage enforces a single invariant, and correctness is the guarantee that a request cannot skip a stage. Stage one is IDENTITY — the request must carry a validated user (getUser/getClaims, not getSession), or it is rejected before any work; this is the boundary from the auth lesson. Stage two is INPUT VALIDATION inside a Server Action — the FormData is untrusted, so it is coerced, normalized, and checked against a schema, and a bad request returns field errors rather than reaching the database. Stage three is AUTHORIZATION, and crucially it lives in the database: the write is subject to the RLS WITH CHECK policy, so an attempt to create a row owned by someone other than auth.uid() is rejected by Postgres itself, not merely by app code — this is why RLS, not a client filter, is the real boundary. Stage four makes the mutation CONSISTENT: after the write, revalidatePath/revalidateTag refresh the cached reads so every surface reflects the new state (and multi-step writes run atomically via an RPC). Stage five is the READ-BACK under the SELECT policy, returning only the user's own rows — the proof of isolation, which must run as the user (never via service_role). Assembled, these stages mean a request missing auth dies at stage one, an invalid one at stage two, an unauthorized write at stage three, and a valid create flows all the way to a consistent, RLS-filtered result. That end-to-end path — validated, authorized, atomic, consistent, isolated — is what "an auth-gated CRUD app enforced by RLS" actually means, and it is the template for every feature you will build on this stack.
capstone-rls-crud.title: Auth-gated CRUD is a pipeline where each stage enforces one invariant
The end-to-end CRUD request path
capstone-rls-crud.subtitle: identity → validate → RLS authorize → mutate → revalidate → RLS read

storyboard.say: A production CRUD write is a pipeline, not one call. Every stage enforces one invariant, and a request cannot skip a stage.
Stage one is identity: the request must carry a validated user from getUser or getClaims, never getSession, or it is rejected.
With an authenticated identity, we enter the Server Action, where the untrusted FormData is coerced and checked against a schema.
Only valid input reaches authorization: the real boundary is the database RLS WITH CHECK policy, not the application code.
Here is the risk: if the row's owner is not auth.uid, RLS rejects the write outright, bouncing a foreign-owner request back.
When owner equals auth.uid, the authorized write commits atomically to the store.
After the write we revalidate the path or tag so cached reads refresh instead of serving stale data.
Finally the read-back is filtered by that same RLS policy, giving a consistent view the user is allowed to see. Composition is correctness.

capstone-rls-crud.title: Compose the auth-gated CRUD pipeline
capstone-rls-crud.summary: Wire the course primitives into one create path: identity check → validate → RLS WITH CHECK authorize → mutate (assigning the DB-style id) → revalidate the cache → RLS-filtered read-back. A valid request flows all the way to a consistent, owner-only read; a foreign-owned write is rejected at authorize; an unauthenticated one dies at identity. Match the exact observable contract, retain a boundary-failure regression, and name the browser, database, RLS, identity, deployment, and production evidence still required. Local output remains practice-only evidence.

capstone-rls-crud.fix:
store.push(newRow);
const visible = store.filter(r => selectPolicy(r, user.id)).map(r => r.id);  // RLS-filtered read-back
capstone-rls-crud.task: The read-back does not apply RLS, so it leaks all rows. Filter the read through the SELECT policy for this user.
capstone-rls-crud.symptom: The composed create returns success and shows the new row, but the read-back also surfaces other users' rows.
capstone-rls-crud.brokenCode:
store.push(newRow);
const visible = store.map(r => r.id);   // read-back ignores the SELECT policy

optionA.text: Assemble validation, RLS WITH CHECK / SELECT policies, and revalidation — each proven in its own lesson — into the pipeline. Every stage is defendable and reusable; the capstone is wiring, not new logic.
optionA.label: Compose primitives

optionB.text: Write the whole create in one function. Fewer files, but the concerns tangle, you cannot test a stage in isolation, and it is exactly where the "read-back skips RLS" leak slips in unnoticed.
optionB.label: One inline handler

capstone-rls-crud.guidance: Compose (A). The course built each primitive alone so the capstone is composition, not invention — which is what makes it testable and lets the same stages power every feature. The monolith (B) is how a skipped stage (an unfiltered read-back, a missing WITH CHECK) hides in the whole.

options: The Server Action rejected an invalid payload and no exception escaped, showing the schema pass guarded every field before the write reached the database.
The create returned success and the row appeared in the UI, which proves the identity, the policy and the revalidation all ran on that one request path.

capstone-rls-crud.question: In the CRUD pipeline, what proves the app is truly auth-gated and isolated, not just working?
capstone-rls-crud.explanation: Success alone can hide the classic leak (read-back skipping RLS). Correct composition means the database rejects an unauthorized write (WITH CHECK) and the read-back — run as the user under the SELECT policy — exposes only their rows, proving authorization and isolation end to end.
